title: An Open Letter to Greta Gerwig
author: Samuel James
summary: Written as a deliberately warm letter to the director rather than a denunciation, James makes the case that casting Meryl Streep as Aslan mutes the fatherhood at the center of Narnia. He opens by praising Gerwig's films and conceding the casting is a mistake but not a devastating one, explicitly trying to keep the disagreement out of the self-righteous register. His argument turns on the claim that Aslan is not one character among many but the reason Narnia exists, so his maleness is not detachable from what makes him special. James is careful to say the issue is not vocal pitch or stereotyped masculinity: the point is that hearing Aslan should make a listener think of a father, and he describes that as arms strong enough to throw a child in the air and soft enough to catch him. He anticipates the objection that tender strength is now likelier to come from women, grants it for argument's sake, and answers with Lewis's own defense of fairy tales as truer than realism. The letter closes by naming two exhaustions it thinks Narnia speaks to, the absence of fatherly tender strength in families and society, and the worship of efficiency that would discard storytelling altogether.
points: Frames the disagreement as a good faith dispute about art, invoking the scissor effect as the thing to avoid rather than a culture-war framing.
Argues Aslan's function as the reason Narnia exists makes his maleness structural rather than incidental, so the change is not comparable to recasting another character.

quotes: I think this was a mistake, but not a devastating one. I think good faith people can disagree about art without such disagreements poisoning our capacity to hear one another
Aslan is, of course, much more than a voice. Most people know that Aslan is a symbol of Jesus.
In other words, Aslan is not just a wise lion. He’s not just a powerful character. He’s the point of Narnia. Aslan himself is the reason Narnia exists

And I would argue that it’s a mistake to abstract what makes him special from his “He-ness.” I’m not at all trying to say that Aslan should have a stereotypically masculine voice. Timber or pitch are not the point. The point is that when people hear Aslan, they should think of a father.

The mysterious mixture of love and dread, joy and seriousness, laughter and honesty, are meant to evoke in us a strong desire for arms that are strong enough to pick us up and throw us in the air, and soft enough to catch us again as tenderly as landing on a pillow.

I think it means something for Aslan to sound like a father. In the same way that the world of Little Women is haunted by a father’s wartime absence, and then comes to life when he appears, the world of Narnia is constantly waiting on its Father to come and make everything and everyone whole again.
I think changing Aslan’s he-ness does two things. It mutes the meaning of his fatherhood and so loses something very close to the soul of Narnia.
